item.title: MACH Energy commits to responsible operation following court ruling
item.dc:creator: Ethan Benedicto
item.description:

Australian Mining.
item.content:encoded:
MACH Energy has reaffirmed its commitment to working with government, regulators and local stakeholders following the High Court’s ruling on its proposed Mount Pleasant mine expansion in New South Wales’ Hunter Valley.

“MACH Energy remains committed to operating responsibly within whatever legal framework the NSW Parliament and the courts establish,” the company said.

“We will continue to actively pursue all available options to ensure the long-term continuity of the Mount Pleasant Operation.”

According to the ruling, planning authorities are now required to consider the emissions caused by burning fossil fuels overseas when approving projects, a decision MACH Energy said it will carefully review to “understand its implications” for future project assessments and environmental approvals.

The High Court case centred on the expansion of the open-cut coal mine near Muswellbrook, which was previously approved by NSW planning authorities in 2022.

MACH Energy said throughout court proceedings its position has been that the “NSW planning system
functions best when decision-makers apply the statutory framework established by the NSW Parliament consistently, transparently and predictably”.

“We advanced this appeal to obtain clarity on important questions regarding the scope of mandatory considerations in environmental decision-making,” the miner said in a statement.

“Clear legal principles benefit proponents, regulators, communities and environmental organisations alike.

“The High Court has now provided that guidance.”

A previous Modification 8 permit provided by the NSW Government in August, Mach Energy said, will allow the mine to continue operating for another six years, increasing permitted coal extraction over that period.

The miner said that while the Modification 8 approval delivered “much-needed continuity” for the project, its focus is now on working constructively with regulators, government, local communities and other stakeholders to further understand the implications of the court ruling.

item.title: Stellar extends tin zone at Heemskirk project
item.dc:creator: Adam Daunt
item.description:

Australian Mining.
item.content:encoded:
Stellar Resources has strengthened the geological case for a larger tin system at its Heemskirk project in Tasmania after drilling intersected high-grade mineralisation north of the existing Severn resource.

Drill hole ZM194 returned 3.9m at 0.82 per cent tin (Sn) from 206.1m, including 2.1m at 1.40 per cent Sn from 206.1m, and 3.7m at 0.41 per cent Sn from 214m, including 0.9m at 1.39 per cent Sn from 216.8m.

The hole was drilled at about 45 degrees to the modelled dip, so true widths are about 70 per cent of the reported intervals.

Stellar said the intersections sit outside the Severn resource at shallower depths, along trend from the high-grade Montana resource, which has 10.4kt of contained tin at 1.54 per cent Sn.

Stellar has also started a follow-up hole with ZS197 to test below ZM194, while a second rig tests the Severn trend north of Montana. Assays are pending from a wedge hole drilled to 850m below the Severn resource.

“Intersecting high-grade tin 150m north of Severn at shallower depths is a major development in our geological understanding that substantially increases our confidence in the potential for Severn and Montana to merge into a single, unified deposit,” Stellar Resources managing director Simon Taylor said.

Heemskirk has a total mineral resource of 13.36Mt at 0.86 per cent Sn for 115.3kt of contained tin, of which 71.9kt is indicated and 43.4kt inferred.

The company said it ranks as the highest-grade undeveloped tin project in Australia and third globally among peer projects

A prefeasibility study (PFS) is evaluating a standalone operation or the use of existing nearby infrastructure, with trade-off studies assessing whether the Severn extensions and Montana could be added to an expanded production profile. Stellar is now targeting PFS completion in the first half of 2027.

“This potential scale expansion offers significant development upside, and we are now undertaking the work to develop the resource at Severn into these new areas to incorporate into the PFS and any future [definitive feasibility study],” Taylor said.

item.title: Best of the best, Tunkillia’s golden finale for Barton Gold
item.dc:creator: Ethan Benedicto
item.description:

The latest batch included 53m at 2.51 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 60m in hole TKB0745, including 2m at 18.25g/t from 72m and 1m at 26.3g/t […]

Australian Mining.
item.content:encoded:
Barton Gold has completed the assay phase of its major Tunkillia resource-upgrade campaign, with final results delivering broad, high-grade intersections inside the South Australian project’s proposed starter pits.

The latest batch included 53m at 2.51 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 60m in hole TKB0745, including 2m at 18.25g/t from 72m and 1m at 26.3g/t from 92m.

Hole TKB0742 returned 21m at 4.13g/t from 61m, including 2m at 29.9g/t from 79m, while TKB0724 intersected 26m at 2.79g/t from 126m, including 1m at 53.5g/t.

Other results included 14m at 3.80g/t from 67m, including 2m at 11g/t, and 17m at 2.26g/t from 116m, including 1m at 20.7g/t.

The assays complete Barton’s 38,760m phase 2 campaign across 311 holes, and together, the phase 1 and phase 2 programs delivered 57,653m of reverse-circulation and diamond drilling across 520 holes.

Barton managing director Alexander Scanlon said the results reinforced both earlier drilling and the interpretation of additional shallow mineralisation.

“We are pleased with the results of Tunkillia’s ‘phase 2’ infill assays, which support the highest-grade results of ‘phase 1’ drilling and the potential for new, shallower zones of high-grade mineralisation within the existing ‘starter pits’,” Scanlon said.

The strongest final assays came from the planned S1 and S2 pits within the main Area 223 open pit, where the current model has an average grade of 1.05g/t gold, the same pits which are intended to provide Tunkillia’s higher-value early production.

Mid-September Phase 2 results had supported a shallow mineralised zone above material already included in the S1 pit model. The new batch completes the dataset needed to test that interpretation through updated geological modelling.

Barton said the latest drilling indicated mineralisation in the starter-pit area may be more vertically controlled than previously modelled, potentially improving the continuity of primary lodes. Mineralised oxidised mafic dyke material was also identified within 18m of surface.

At Area 51, phase 2 drilling confirmed a thick, higher-grade shoot extending approximately 250m north and 200m south across separate sections. The mineralisation remains open to the south and west, and drilling at Area 223 North also identified mineralisation at or beyond the limits used in the previous pit profile.

The reported intersections are downhole lengths, and their effect on Tunkillia’s resource, mine plan and economics has not yet been determined.

Tunkillia currently hosts 1.6 million ounces of gold and 3.1 million ounces of silver, and Barton has begun remodelling the deposit, with an updated gold mineral resource expected first and an updated silver resource planned for the first quarter of 2027.

“We are now remodelling all Tunkillia mineralisation with the benefit of nearly 58,000m additional drilling since last year,” Scanlon said.

“A JORC resources update for gold is pending, and a JORC update for silver and a pre-feasibility study are planned for the first quarter of the 2027 calendar year.”

The updates will feed into the pre-feasibility study being led by GR Engineering Services.

Barton’s May 2025 optimised scoping study outlined a potential operation producing about 120,000 ounces of gold and 250,000 ounces of silver annually, with a $1.4 billion unlevered pre-tax net present value, a 73.2 per cent internal rate of return and a payback period of about 0.8 years under the study assumptions.

Those projections pre-date the latest drilling and remain subject to the PFS and further technical work.

The development program is also moving through approvals. The South Australian Government recently approved Tunkillia’s environmental scoping report, establishing the terms of reference for environmental studies, consultation and other work required for the mining lease process.

Barton is progressing flora, fauna, water and cultural heritage programs alongside tailings, infrastructure, accommodation and renewable-energy studies.

The company intends to lodge a mining lease application after the PFS, which remains targeted for the first quarter of 2027.

item.title: BHP offloads Kambalda concentrator to Gold Fields
item.dc:creator: Adam Daunt
item.description:

Under agreements announced on October 7, completion is expected during calendar year 2027, subject […]

Australian Mining.
item.content:encoded:
BHP has agreed to sell its idled Kambalda Nickel Concentrator (KNC), along with a package of tenements and mineralisation rights, to Gold Fields, in a deal that hands the Western Australian plant to a gold miner already operating in the region.

Under agreements announced on October 7, completion is expected during calendar year 2027, subject to conditions including regulatory approvals. BHP said the financial terms are confidential.

Gold Fields said it would assess the assets, including the concentrator’s long-term use for gold and nickel processing, and engage Traditional Owners, government, local communities and industry partners.

“These are highly strategic assets located in a region where we have operated and invested for many years, and we see significant potential to explore future opportunities,” Gold Fields senior vice president of operations for Australia Craig Bradshaw said. 

Gold Fields said gold production remained its core focus, with “no changes to our operations or workforce as a result of this acquisition”.

It operates the St Ives mine near Kambalda and three other gold mines in Western Australia’s eastern Goldfields.

BHP suspended its WA Nickel assets in July 2024, citing “oversupply in the global nickel market”.

The remaining assets, including the refinery, smelter and mines, stay suspended, and BHP intends to review that decision by February 2027, assessing divestment, continued suspension, restart or closure.

BHP vice president WA Nickel Annabelle Blom called the sale “a positive outcome” that “provides certainty for our employees, the Goldfields region and the local community”.

“The review process continues and we remain committed to engaging closely with our people and communities to keep them informed of progress and decisions,” she said.

item.title: Finlayson calls Northern Star approach ‘opportunistic’
item.dc:creator: Engel Schmidl
item.description:
Genesis Minerals executive chair Raleigh Finlayson has cast doubt on whether Gold Fields’ rejected approach for Northern Star Resources will succeed, describing the proposal as opportunistic and suggesting a larger cash component would be needed. Speaking at the Melbourne Mining Club, Finlayson questioned aspects of the proposal and its estimated synergies, while pointing to further […]

Australian Mining.
item.content:encoded:
Genesis Minerals executive chair Raleigh Finlayson has cast doubt on whether Gold Fields’ rejected approach for Northern Star Resources will succeed, describing the proposal as opportunistic and suggesting a larger cash component would be needed.

Speaking at the Melbourne Mining Club, Finlayson questioned aspects of the proposal and its estimated synergies, while pointing to further opportunities for consolidation across Australia’s gold sector.

“I don’t think it will,” Finlayson told the audience when asked if Northern Star could fall into foreign ownership following the recent bid by South African-based Gold Fields.

“So I think it’s an opportunistic bid.”

Finlayson drew a comparison with Gold Fields’ approach to its Gold Road acquisition and said the amount of Gold Fields scrip involved could present an obstacle when pursuing a larger target.

“It’s going to require Gold Fields… so they need to be increasing the cash amount for that to happen.”

Northern Star’s board unanimously rejected the confidential September 14 proposal, citing undervaluation and high completion risk.

The offer valued Northern Star at around $38 billion based on Gold Fields’ September 11 closing share price, representing a 22 per cent premium to Northern Star’s closing price that day.

Approximately 73 per cent of the implied consideration comprised new Gold Fields shares, with cash accounting for the remaining 27 per cent. Northern Star shareholders would have held approximately 33 per cent of the combined entity.

Northern Star chairman Michael Chaney said the proposal sought to acquire the company at a price below its fundamental value and ahead of key growth milestones, including commissioning and ramp-up of KCGM’s Fimiston Mill.

Gold Fields said Northern Star’s assets complemented its portfolio and estimated potential synergies of $4–5 billion.

Finlayson said those estimates deserved scepticism because Gold Fields had not conducted due diligence on Northern Star. He acknowledged potential tax benefits could be substantial, while noting he had not reviewed the books.

Still a Northern Star shareholder, although with a “slightly less” holding than previously, Finlayson said the company had historically retained its production and assets, with few noticeable divestments.

He would consider Northern Star assets if they fitted Genesis’ strategy, which he said remains disciplined and focused on Australian gold.

More broadly, Finlayson expects consolidation and asset sales to create opportunities for operators prepared to invest in overlooked operations.

“Great opportunities will occur for companies to take those [non-core assets] and put a bit more love into those assets.”

He described the Genesis–Vault merger as an obvious strategic fit, emphasising practical cost savings over hypothetical synergies. Genesis’ growth focus remains its existing district and organic opportunities in the Leonora district of Western Australia, rather than pursuing scale for its own sake.

Finlayson’s broader concern is whether the sector will invest sufficiently in exploration as resources are depleted and discoveries become deeper and harder to find.

He warned inadequate funding could push exploration investment offshore, arguing companies must balance exploration and development spending with sustainable shareholder returns.

That balance, alongside disciplined capital allocation, underpins his outlook for continued growth at Genesis and further opportunities across the Australian gold industry.
